lessons.title: Income Statement of a Sole Trader
lessons.markdown:
# Income Statement of a Sole Trader

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Define a sole trader and explain the purpose of the income statement.
2. Distinguish the trading section (gross profit) from the profit and loss section (net profit).
3. Compute cost of sales from opening stock, purchases, returns, carriage inwards and closing stock.
4. Classify items correctly between the trading account and the profit and loss account.
5. Prepare a trading and profit and loss account in vertical format from given data.
6. Treat special items correctly: abnormal losses, goods in transit, goods on approval, and free samples.

---

## 1. The Sole Trader and the Need for Financial Statements

A sole trader — also called a sole proprietorship — is a business owned and run by one individual, with no legal distinction between the owner and the business. You own it entirely, you grow it, and its success or failure rests on you. You are entitled to all the profit it makes.

At the end of each financial year, every business must answer one question: **did we make a profit or a loss?** This is done in two stages:

1. **Finding gross profit (or gross loss)** — in the trading account section.
2. **Finding net profit (or net loss)** — in the profit and loss account section.

The trial balance provides the essential input. In practice the two sections are combined into a single report — the **income statement** — but examiners still expect you to know which items belong to each stage.

## 2. Stage 1: Determining Gross Profit

Gross profit is the difference between the **sale proceeds of the period** and the **cost of the goods actually sold**. No deduction of any kind — general, administrative, or selling and distribution expenses — is made at this stage. If sale proceeds exceed the cost of goods sold, there is a gross profit; if cost exceeds proceeds, a gross loss.

### Items debited (the cost side)

- **Opening stock** — the value of goods on hand at the end of the previous year, which becomes the opening stock of the current year.
- **Purchases** — goods bought for resale, cash or credit. Adjust for:
  - purchases of **capital assets** wrongly included (deduct them);
  - goods taken for **personal use/drawings** (exclude — treat as drawings);
  - goods **in transit** at year-end (debit stock-in-transit, credit supplier);
  - goods received on **consignment, on approval or hire purchase** (exclude);
  - cost of goods **sent on consignment** (deduct from purchases).
- **Returns outwards (purchases returns)** — shown as a deduction from purchases (or on the credit side).
- **Direct expenses** — expenses incurred in purchasing, procuring or producing the goods and bringing them to the point of sale. The classic exam item is **carriage inwards**.

### Items credited (the revenue side)

- **Sales** — cash and credit sales of the goods the business deals in. Exclude: sale of old fixed assets, goods sent on approval (until approved), free samples, and any sales tax included in the figure.
- **Returns inwards (sales returns)** — deducted from sales (or shown on the debit side).
- **Abnormal loss of stock** — stock lost through fire, theft or accident is credited in full to the trading account, because the trading account is prepared under *normal* conditions and has no place for abnormal events. (The loss itself is then dealt with in the profit and loss account.)
- **Closing stock** — goods unsold at year-end, valued at **cost or market price, whichever is lower**. The trial balance normally does *not* include closing stock, so it is brought in by: `Dr. Closing stock account / Cr. Income statement`. If closing stock already appears in the trial balance, it goes **only** to the statement of financial position.

### The cost-of-sales formula (memorise this)

```
Opening stock
+ Purchases
+ Carriage inwards (direct expenses)
− Returns outwards
= Cost of goods available for sale
− Closing stock
= COST OF SALES
```

```
Net sales (sales − returns inwards) − Cost of sales = GROSS PROFIT
```

## 3. Worked Example: Trading Account

**Question:** From the following details, draw up the trading account of Mr. Karanja for the year ended 31 December 2025, his first year in business.

| Item | Sh. |
|---|---|
| Carriage inwards | 134,000 |
| Returns outwards | 99,000 |
| Returns inwards | 178,000 |
| Sales | 7,748,400 |
| Purchases | 6,666,600 |
| Stock at 31 December 2025 | 1,497,800 |

**Solution:**

```
                                    Mr. Karanja
                 Trading Account for the year ended 31 December 2025
                                                    Sh.            Sh.
Sales                                            7,748,400
Less: Returns inwards                             (178,000)
Net sales                                                        7,570,400
Less: Cost of sales
  Purchases                          6,666,600
  Add: Carriage inwards                 134,000
                                     6,800,600
  Less: Returns outwards                (99,000)
  Cost of goods available for sale   6,701,600
  Less: Closing stock               (1,497,800)
  Cost of sales                                                 (5,203,800)
Gross profit                                                     2,366,600
```

Check: 7,570,400 − 5,203,800 = 2,366,600. ✓ (There is no opening stock — it is his first year in business.)

## 4. Stage 2: Determining Net Profit

After gross profit is found, all remaining **indirect** expenses and losses are charged on the debit side, and all other incomes on the credit side:

**Debited (expenses and losses):**
- Management/administrative expenses — office salaries, office rent, printing and stationery, telephone.
- Selling and distribution expenses — salesmen's salaries and commission, advertising, packaging, **carriage outwards**, bad debts.
- Maintenance expenses — repairs and renewals of office fixed assets.
- Financial expenses — interest on loans, bank charges, discount allowed.
- Abnormal losses — e.g., stock lost by fire not covered by insurance, loss on sale of machinery.
- Depreciation of non-current assets.

**Credited (other incomes):**
- Gross profit brought down.
- Other income — discount received, commission received.
- Non-trading income — interest on bank deposits, dividends, rent of property let out, profit on sale of fixed assets.
- Abnormal gains — e.g., profit on sale of a fixed asset (shown separately).

Net profit = total credits − total debits. If debits exceed credits, it is a net loss. The balancing figure is entered on the smaller side, after which both sides agree.

## 5. Special Treatments Examiners Love

- **Carriage inwards vs. carriage outwards:** carriage *inwards* is a direct expense (trading account, part of cost of sales); carriage *outwards* is a selling expense (profit and loss account). Mixing them up is a classic mark-loser.
- **Returns:** returns *inwards* reduce sales; returns *outwards* reduce purchases. Always net them off — never add them.
- **Abnormal loss of stock:** credit the trading account in full (normal conditions only), then charge the loss to the profit and loss account. If insured, recognise the insurance claim as an asset until received.
- **Goods sent on approval:** not a sale until the customer approves. Cancel the sale (Dr. Sales / Cr. Debtors at selling price) and add the goods back to closing stock at cost.
- **Free samples:** advertisement expense — `Dr. Advertisement / Cr. Purchases`, then charge advertisement to the profit and loss account.
- **Drawings in kind:** goods taken by the owner reduce purchases at cost (`Dr. Drawings / Cr. Purchases`).

![Income statement format](../illustrations/income-statement-format.png)

## 6. Common Exam Traps

1. **Carriage inwards vs. carriage outwards** — the single most confused pair in this topic. Inwards = cost of sales; outwards = selling expense.
2. **Adding returns instead of deducting them** — returns inwards reduce sales; returns outwards reduce purchases.
3. **Putting closing stock in the trial balance section** — closing stock from *additional information* is credited to the trading account AND shown as a current asset. (If it were already in the trial balance, it would go to the statement of financial position only.)
4. **Charging indirect expenses in the trading account** — salaries, rent, insurance and depreciation belong below gross profit, never above it.
5. **Forgetting that sales excludes fixed-asset disposals** — selling an old van is not "sales"; any profit or loss goes to the profit and loss account separately.
6. **Treating abnormal losses as normal cost of sales** — they are credited out of the trading account and charged below the line.

## 7. Key Terms (Flashcards)

- **Sole trader** — A business owned and run by one individual with no legal distinction between owner and business.
- **Income statement** — The combined trading and profit and loss account showing gross profit and net profit for a period.
- **Gross profit** — Net sales minus cost of sales; profit before deducting indirect expenses.
- **Net profit** — Gross profit plus other incomes minus all indirect expenses; the final result for the period.
- **Cost of sales** — Opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − returns outwards − closing stock.
- **Direct expenses** — Expenses of purchasing/procuring goods and bringing them to the point of sale (e.g., carriage inwards).
- **Returns inwards** — Goods returned by customers; deducted from sales.
- **Returns outwards** — Goods returned to suppliers; deducted from purchases.
- **Abnormal loss** — Stock lost through fire, theft or accident; credited to the trading account and charged to profit and loss.
- **Closing stock** — Unsold goods at year-end, valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower.

## 8. Lesson Summary

- The income statement answers in two stages: gross profit (trading section) then net profit (profit and loss section).
- Cost of sales = opening stock + purchases + carriage inwards − returns outwards − closing stock.
- Only direct items sit above gross profit; all indirect expenses and other incomes sit below it.
- Special items — abnormal losses, approval sales, free samples, drawings in kind — each have a fixed treatment you must memorise.

## 9. Exam Day Tips

- Write the cost-of-sales formula at the top of your answer page before you start — it prevents omission errors under pressure.
- Always compute **net sales** and **net purchases** first; then the rest is mechanical.
- Label every figure (Sh.) and show workings for closing stock and adjustments — method marks are generous.
- In combined income statements, draw a clear line (or subtotal) at gross profit so the examiner sees both stages.

---

*Next: Lesson 2 — the Statement of Financial Position: grouping, marshalling, and the accounting equation in exam format.*

lessons.title: Statement of Financial Position
lessons.markdown:
# Statement of Financial Position

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Define the statement of financial position and state its purpose.
2. Distinguish the statement of financial position from the trial balance (seven points of difference).
3. Classify assets correctly: non-current, intangible, current, liquid/quick, fictitious, wasting and contingent.
4. Classify liabilities into non-current, current and contingent.
5. Apply grouping and marshalling (order of liquidity vs. order of permanence).
6. Prepare a statement of financial position for a sole trader in vertical format, with capital properly reconciled.
7. State the limitations of financial statements, including the impact of accounting policies.

---

## 1. What the Statement of Financial Position Is

The statement of financial position (formerly called the balance sheet) is a summary of the financial balances of a business as at a **specific date** — typically the end of the financial year. It lists assets, liabilities and the owner's equity. It is often described as a *"snapshot of the financial condition"* of the business: it shows what the business owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owner.

Key structural facts:

- It is prepared **after** the income statement (net profit is needed to update capital).
- It contains only balances of accounts that have **not been squared up** — real and personal accounts (assets, liabilities, capital). All nominal accounts (incomes and expenses) have already been closed to the income statement.
- It must **balance**: Total assets = Capital + Liabilities (the accounting equation).
- It also absorbs all **adjustments** affecting real or personal accounts — accruals, prepayments, depreciation, provisions.

## 2. Trial Balance vs. Statement of Financial Position

Examiners frequently ask for this distinction. Learn these seven points:

| | Trial balance | Statement of financial position |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Purpose | Checks arithmetical accuracy of the books | Reveals the financial position of the business |
| 2. What it proves | Total debits = total credits | Total assets = liabilities + equity |
| 3. Timing | Prepared **before** the income statement | Prepared **after** the income statement |
| 4. Closing stock | Not included | Included on the assets side |
| 5. Accruals/prepayments | Do not appear | Accrued expenses appear as liabilities; prepayments and accrued income as assets |
| 6. Columns | "Debit" and "credit" columns | "Assets" and "liabilities/equity" sides |
| 7. Coverage | Balances of **all** accounts (real, nominal, personal) | Balances of **assets and liabilities only** |

## 3. Classification of Assets

- **Non-current (fixed) assets** — acquired to produce goods or render services, not held for resale: land and buildings, plant and machinery, furniture and fixtures, motor vehicles. Shown at cost less accumulated depreciation ("gross block" vs. "net block").
- **Intangible assets** — no physical existence but long-lasting and income-generating: goodwill, trademarks, copyrights, patents.
- **Current assets** — cash or assets convertible into cash within the normal operating cycle (about a year): stock, debtors, bills receivable, bank, cash in hand, prepaid expenses. Also called floating or circulating assets.
- **Liquid (quick) assets** — current assets convertible into cash almost immediately without loss: current assets **minus** stock and prepayments.
- **Fictitious assets** — worthless items representing unamortised past costs: preliminary expenses, discount on issue of shares/debentures, debit balance of the income statement. Written off to the income statement over time.
- **Wasting assets** — natural resources that deplete with use: timber, coal, oil wells, mineral deposits.
- **Contingent assets** — probable assets depending on a future event (e.g., a pending court case over property). Shown by **footnote only**, never in the statement itself.

## 4. Classification of Liabilities

- **Non-current (long-term) liabilities** — obligations not due within the normal operating cycle: debentures, long-term bank loans, mortgages.
- **Current liabilities** — payable within the accounting year: trade creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft, outstanding (accrued) expenses, short-term loans.
- **Contingent liabilities** — potential obligations depending on a future event: bills discounted, guarantees given, pending lawsuits. A journal entry is made only if the liability is **probable and estimable**; if merely *possible*, disclose by note; if *remote*, do nothing.

## 5. Grouping and Marshalling

Preparation involves two steps:

1. **Grouping** — items of a similar nature are brought under one head (e.g., stock, debtors, bank and cash under "Current assets").
2. **Marshalling** — assets and liabilities are arranged in a logical order. Two methods:
   - **Order of liquidity** — most liquid first (cash → debtors → stock → fixed assets); liabilities in the order they fall due.
   - **Order of permanence** — the reverse: fixed assets first, then current assets; after capital, long-term, then current liabilities. **This is the commonly used method** and the one KASNEB expects.

## 6. Worked Example: Statement of Financial Position

**Question (extract):** After preparing his income statement for the year ended 31 December 2025, S. Mwangi's books show: freehold premises at cost Sh.2,600,000; motor vehicle at cost Sh.1,280,000 (accumulated depreciation Sh.128,000); fixtures at cost Sh.576,000 (accumulated depreciation Sh.28,800); stock Sh.1,760,000; debtors Sh.1,808,400 (provision for bad debts Sh.45,210); bank Sh.1,056,400; cash Sh.56,800; prepayments (rates Sh.25,600 + unexpired insurance Sh.4,000) Sh.29,600; creditors Sh.2,169,000; capital Sh.5,920,000; drawings Sh.1,200,000; net profit Sh.2,076,190.

**Solution:**

```
                                         S. Mwangi
                      Statement of Financial Position as at 31 December 2025
                                    Cost         Acc. Dep.        NBV
                                    Sh.            Sh.            Sh.
Non-current assets
  Freehold premises            2,600,000              –        2,600,000
  Motor vehicle                1,280,000        128,000        1,152,000
  Fixtures and fittings          576,000         28,800          547,200
                               4,456,000        156,800        4,299,200
Current assets
  Stock                                                        1,760,000
  Debtors                        1,808,400
  Less: Provision for bad debts   (45,210)                     1,763,190
  Bank                                                         1,056,400
  Cash                                                            56,800
  Prepayments                                                     29,600
                                                               4,665,990
Total assets                                                   8,965,190

Financed by:
  Capital                                                      5,920,000
  Add: Net profit                                              2,076,190
  Less: Drawings                                              (1,200,000)
                                                               6,796,190
Current liabilities
  Creditors                                                    2,169,000
Total equity and liabilities                                   8,965,190
```

Verification: 4,299,200 + 4,665,990 = 8,965,190; 6,796,190 + 2,169,000 = 8,965,190. ✓ The statement balances.

> Note on the capital section: the owner's interest is always shown as **Capital + Net profit − Drawings** (drawings reduce capital). Income tax paid by a sole trader is treated as drawings, never as a business expense.

## 7. Limitations of Financial Statements

The income statement and statement of financial position are full of information — but the message is not infallible. The study text highlights these limitations:

1. **Choice of accounting policies** — management chooses among policies for stock valuation, depreciation, provisions and R&D; identical businesses can report different profits.
2. **One set of statements, many users** — owners, workers, investors, creditors and the government all want different information; a single set cannot serve everyone equally.
3. **Only monetary items appear** — worker morale, management quality, customer loyalty and R&D effort cannot be quantified and are omitted.
4. **Human resources are not recognised** — the most important asset of all cannot yet be meaningfully valued in the statements.
5. **Inflation distorts values** — asset values fall out of line with current prices, so profitability measured on historical cost can be misleading and partly illusory.

![Statement of financial position format](../illustrations/statement-of-financial-position-format.png)

## 8. Common Exam Traps

1. **Forgetting to add net profit to capital** — the statement of financial position is prepared *after* the income statement; capital must be updated.
2. **Adding drawings instead of deducting them** — drawings always reduce the owner's capital.
3. **Showing accumulated depreciation as a liability** — it is a *deduction from the asset's cost* (or shown on the "liabilities side" only in the book's alternative presentation — the deduction format is safer and standard).
4. **Including nominal account balances** — salaries, rent paid, discount allowed belong in the income statement, never in the statement of financial position.
5. **Omitting adjustments** — accrued expenses (liability), prepaid expenses (asset), and provisions against debtors must all appear.
6. **Marshalling in the wrong order** — KASNEB expects the order of permanence (non-current assets first), not liquidity order.

## 9. Key Terms (Flashcards)

- **Statement of financial position** — A statement of assets, liabilities and equity as at a specific date; a snapshot of financial condition.
- **Accounting equation** — Assets = Capital + Liabilities; the statement must always balance on this.
- **Grouping** — Bringing items of a similar nature under one head in the statement.
- **Marshalling** — Arranging assets and liabilities in a logical order (liquidity or permanence).
- **Non-current assets** — Assets acquired for use in the business, not for resale, held long-term.
- **Current assets** — Cash and assets convertible to cash within the normal operating cycle.
- **Quick (liquid) assets** — Current assets minus stock and prepayments.
- **Non-current liabilities** — Obligations not due within the normal operating cycle.
- **Current liabilities** — Obligations payable within the accounting year.
- **Contingent liability** — A potential obligation depending on a future event; journalised only if probable and estimable, otherwise disclosed or ignored.
- **Drawings** — Cash or goods taken by the owner for personal use; deducted from capital.

## 10. Lesson Summary

- The statement of financial position is prepared after the income statement and contains only asset, liability and capital balances.
- Assets and liabilities are grouped by nature and marshalled — normally in order of permanence.
- Capital is always presented as: opening capital + net profit − drawings.
- The statement must satisfy Assets = Capital + Liabilities; use this as your arithmetic check.
- Financial statements have real limitations: policy choices, monetary-only measurement, and inflation effects.

## 11. Exam Day Tips

- Before writing, list every trial balance item and mark it "IS" (income statement) or "SOFP" (statement of financial position) — this one habit prevents most classification errors.
- Always finish with the balancing check: total assets vs. total equity + liabilities. If they differ, an item is missing or misclassified.
- Show the non-current assets as a Cost / Accumulated depreciation / Net book value schedule — it earns presentation marks.
- Memorise the seven trial-balance-vs-SOFP differences; they are a ready-made 7-mark question.

---

*Next: Lesson 3 — Adjustments and Worked Examples: accruals, prepayments, depreciation, bad debts and provisions, with a full trial-balance-to-statements question.*

lessons.title: Adjustments and Worked Examples
lessons.markdown:
# Adjustments and Worked Examples

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Explain the accrual (matching) concept and why year-end adjustments are needed.
2. Adjust for outstanding (accrued) expenses and prepaid expenses, with correct double entries.
3. Provide for depreciation using the straight-line and reducing-balance methods, including pro-rata charges.
4. Write off bad debts and create or adjust a provision for bad debts (both TB situations).
5. Adjust for drawings in kind, accrued loan interest, and provisions for discount on debtors.
6. Prepare a complete income statement and statement of financial position from a trial balance with additional information.

---

## 1. Why Adjustments Exist: the Matching Concept

The trial balance captures what was *paid or received* during the year. But profit must reflect what was *incurred or earned* in the year — the accrual (matching) concept. Four situations force adjustments:

| Situation | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Expense incurred but not yet paid (outstanding/accrued) | Add to the expense; recognise a current liability |
| Expense paid but not yet incurred (prepaid) | Deduct from the expense; recognise a current asset |
| Asset consumed during the year (depreciation) | Charge the expired portion to the income statement |
| Probable future loss (provision) | Charge the expected loss now (prudence concept) |

## 2. Accrued (Outstanding) Expenses

An accrued expense has been incurred but not paid by year-end — e.g., December salaries paid in January.

```
Dr. Expense account
    Cr. Outstanding/accrued expenses account
```

Effect: the expense in the income statement **increases**; a **current liability** appears in the statement of financial position.

*Example:* Salaries paid during the year Sh.1,350,000; salaries for December Sh.90,000 unpaid at 31 December. Income statement charge = Sh.1,440,000; accrued salaries Sh.90,000 sit under current liabilities.

## 3. Prepaid Expenses

A prepaid expense has been paid but not yet incurred — e.g., rent paid covering the first months of next year.

```
Dr. Prepaid expenses account (asset)
    Cr. Expense account
```

Effect: the expense in the income statement **decreases**; a **current asset** appears in the statement of financial position.

*Example:* Rent paid Sh.480,000 includes Sh.60,000 relating to next year. Income statement charge = Sh.420,000; prepaid rent Sh.60,000 is a current asset.

## 4. Depreciation

Depreciation is the permanent, continuing fall in the value of a non-current asset from use and the passage of time. Each year a portion of the asset's cost expires and must be charged to the income statement.

**Journal entries** (asset maintained at cost, the normal exam case):

```
Dr. Depreciation account
    Cr. Provision for depreciation account
Dr. Income statement
    Cr. Depreciation account
```

**Methods (per the study text):**
- **Straight-line (fixed instalment):** a fixed percentage of *cost* each year. 10% on cost of Sh.800,000 = Sh.80,000 p.a.
- **Reducing (diminishing) balance:** a fixed percentage of the *net book value* each year. 20% on NBV of Sh.1,000,000 = Sh.200,000 in year 1; 20% of Sh.800,000 = Sh.160,000 in year 2.
- **Pro-rata:** when an asset is bought or sold mid-year, charge depreciation for the months held (e.g., 20% × cost × 3/12).

**Exam rule:** no adjustment is needed for depreciation that *already appears in the trial balance* — it is charged to the income statement as it stands. And accumulated depreciation is shown as a **deduction from the asset's cost**, never as a liability.

## 5. Bad Debts and Provisions

**Bad debts written off** (a debtor will never pay):

```
Dr. Bad debts account
    Cr. Debtor's personal account
Dr. Income statement
    Cr. Bad debts account
```

A bad debt already in the trial balance goes straight to the income statement — no further adjustment.

**Provision for bad debts** (an estimate of debtors who *may* not pay — the prudence concept):

- *Situation 1 — no provision in the trial balance:* `Dr. Income statement / Cr. Provision for bad debts` for the full new provision.
- *Situation 2 — a provision exists in the trial balance:* compute the new required provision and compare:
  - New > old → charge the **increase**: `Dr. Income statement / Cr. Provision` (increase).
  - New < old → credit the **decrease**: `Dr. Provision / Cr. Income statement` (decrease).

Only the **new** provision is shown in the statement of financial position, deducted from debtors.

*Example:* Debtors Sh.950,000; provision required at 5% = Sh.47,500; old provision Sh.40,000 → increase of Sh.7,500 charged to the income statement; debtors shown net as Sh.902,500.

**Provision for discount on debtors:** debtors who pay promptly earn cash discount, so debtors are overstated. The provision is computed on debtors *after* deducting bad debts written off and the bad-debt provision: `Dr. Income statement / Cr. Provision for discount on debtors`, deducted from debtors in the statement of financial position. (Note: in practice, no reserve is made for discount on *creditors*, out of conservatism.)

## 6. Other Standard Adjustments

- **Drawings in kind** (goods taken by the owner): `Dr. Drawings / Cr. Purchases` at cost — reduces cost of sales and increases drawings.
- **Accrued loan interest:** `Dr. Interest on loan / Cr. Accrued interest (or Loan account)` — the full year's interest is charged; the unpaid portion is a current liability.
- **Income tax of a sole trader:** treated as **drawings**, never as a business expense (`Dr. Drawings / Cr. Cash`).
- **Goods on approval / free samples / abnormal losses:** as covered in Lesson 1 — cancel approval sales at selling price, add back to stock at cost; free samples are advertisement (`Dr. Advertisement / Cr. Purchases`).

## 7. Full Worked Example (Verified)

**Question:** The following trial balance was extracted from the books of D. Achieng, a sole trader, as at 31 December 2025:

| | Dr. Sh. | Cr. Sh. |
|---|---|---|
| Premises at cost | 3,000,000 | |
| Equipment at cost | 800,000 | |
| Provision for depreciation – equipment | | 240,000 |
| Stock, 1 January 2025 | 420,000 | |
| Purchases | 4,600,000 | |
| Sales | | 6,500,000 |
| Returns inwards | 90,000 | |
| Returns outwards | | 70,000 |
| Carriage inwards | 110,000 | |
| Carriage outwards | 60,000 | |
| Salaries | 1,350,000 | |
| Rent | 480,000 | |
| Insurance | 120,000 | |
| Discount allowed | 45,000 | |
| Discount received | | 60,000 |
| Bad debts written off | 30,000 | |
| Provision for bad debts | | 40,000 |
| Debtors | 950,000 | |
| Creditors | | 720,000 |
| Bank | 640,000 | |
| Cash | 85,000 | |
| Drawings | 300,000 | |
| Capital | | 4,500,000 |
| Bank loan | | 1,000,000 |
| Interest on loan paid | 50,000 | |
| **Totals** | **13,130,000** | **13,130,000** |

**Additional information:**
1. Closing stock at 31 December 2025: Sh.510,000.
2. Rent prepaid at year-end: Sh.60,000.
3. Salaries accrued at year-end: Sh.90,000.
4. Depreciation on equipment: 10% per annum on cost.
5. Provision for bad debts to be 5% of debtors.
6. Insurance prepaid: Sh.15,000.
7. The owner took goods costing Sh.40,000 for personal use (not recorded).
8. The bank loan of Sh.1,000,000 carries interest at 10% per annum.

**Solution — Income statement for the year ended 31 December 2025:**

```
Net sales: 6,500,000 − 90,000 (returns inwards)                       6,410,000
Cost of sales:
  Opening stock                                           420,000
  Purchases 4,600,000 − 40,000 (drawings in kind)        4,560,000
  Carriage inwards                                        110,000
                                                        5,090,000
  Less: Returns outwards                                   (70,000)  5,020,000
  Less: Closing stock                                    (510,000) (4,510,000)
Gross profit                                                          1,900,000
Add: Discount received                                                   60,000
                                                                      1,960,000
Less: Expenses
  Carriage outwards                                         60,000
  Salaries 1,350,000 + 90,000 accrued                    1,440,000
  Rent 480,000 − 60,000 prepaid                              420,000
  Insurance 120,000 − 15,000 prepaid                          105,000
  Discount allowed                                            45,000
  Bad debts written off                                       30,000
  Increase in provision (47,500 − 40,000)                       7,500
  Depreciation: equipment 10% × 800,000                        80,000
  Interest on loan 50,000 + 50,000 accrued (10% × 1,000,000)  100,000 (2,287,500)
Net loss                                                             (327,500)
```

Check: 1,960,000 − 2,287,500 = −327,500. ✓ (A net loss — expenses exceeded gross income; always read what the numbers tell you.)

**Solution — Statement of financial position as at 31 December 2025:**

```
Non-current assets                              Cost         Acc. dep.      NBV
Premises                                   3,000,000             –      3,000,000
Equipment                                    800,000         320,000       480,000
                                                                       3,480,000
Current assets
  Stock                                                                     510,000
  Debtors 950,000 − provision 47,500 (5%)                                    902,500
  Bank                                                                      640,000
  Cash                                                                       85,000
  Prepayments (rent 60,000 + insurance 15,000)                                75,000
                                                                        2,212,500
Total assets                                                                5,692,500

Financed by:
  Capital                                                                 4,500,000
  Less: Net loss                                                           (327,500)
  Less: Drawings (300,000 + 40,000 goods)                                  (340,000)
                                                                          3,832,500
Non-current liabilities
  Bank loan                                                               1,000,000
Current liabilities
  Creditors                                                                 720,000
  Accrued salaries                                                           90,000
  Accrued loan interest                                                      50,000
                                                                            860,000
Total equity and liabilities                                              5,692,500
```

Final check: 3,480,000 + 2,212,500 = 5,692,500; 3,832,500 + 1,000,000 + 860,000 = 5,692,500. ✓ The statement balances.

## 8. Common Exam Traps

1. **Adding prepayments to expenses** instead of deducting them — prepaid means "paid too much this year": deduct.
2. **Forgetting the accrued expense in BOTH places** — it increases the income-statement charge AND creates a current liability. Missing either side loses marks.
3. **Using the old provision figure in the statement of financial position** — only the NEW provision is deducted from debtors; the difference goes to the income statement.
4. **Depreciating on cost when the policy says reducing balance** (or vice versa) — read the additional information word by word.
5. **Treating drawings in kind at selling price** — always at cost, and remember to increase drawings too.
6. **Charging a full year's depreciation on assets bought or sold mid-year** — apply pro-rata unless told otherwise.
7. **Forgetting interest accrued on loans** — compare interest paid with rate × loan × time; the shortfall is accrued.

![Adjustments flow](../illustrations/adjustments-flow.png)

## 9. Key Terms (Flashcards)

- **Accrual (matching) concept** — Income and expenses are recognised when incurred/earned, not when cash changes hands.
- **Accrued (outstanding) expense** — An expense incurred but not yet paid; a current liability.
- **Prepaid expense** — An expense paid but not yet incurred; a current asset.
- **Depreciation** — The permanent fall in value of a non-current asset from use and time; charged to the income statement each year.
- **Straight-line method** — Depreciation at a fixed percentage of cost each year.
- **Reducing-balance method** — Depreciation at a fixed percentage of net book value each year.
- **Pro-rata depreciation** — Charging depreciation for the part of the year the asset was held.
- **Bad debt** — A debtor balance that will never be recovered; written off to the income statement.
- **Provision for bad debts** — An estimate of doubtful debts charged to profit under the prudence concept; deducted from debtors.
- **Drawings in kind** — Goods taken by the owner for personal use; credited to purchases at cost and debited to drawings.

## 10. Lesson Summary

- Accruals add to expenses (and create liabilities); prepayments reduce expenses (and create assets).
- Depreciation: straight-line on cost, reducing-balance on NBV, pro-rata for part-years; accumulated depreciation is deducted from cost.
- Bad debts written off go straight to the income statement; provisions compare new vs. old, with only the difference hitting profit and only the new figure deducted from debtors.
- Always verify: every adjustment hits TWO places (income statement + statement of financial position), and the final statement must balance.

## 11. Exam Day Tips

- Build an "adjustments table" before writing the statements: one row per additional-information item, with columns for income-statement effect and SOFP effect.
- Compute net sales, net purchases, new provisions and depreciation workings FIRST — then the statements are purely mechanical.
- Show every working (W1, W2...) — method marks rescue you even if a number slips.
- End with the accounting-equation check: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. If it fails, find the missing adjustment before moving on.

---

mcqs.question: Which of the following best defines a sole trader?
options: A) A business owned by shareholders with limited liability
B) A business owned and run by one individual with no legal distinction between owner and business
C) An association of two or more persons carrying on business for profit
D) A business owned by the government
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because the study text defines a sole trader (sole proprietorship) as owned and run by one individual, with no legal distinction between owner and business.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) describes a limited company.
- C) describes a partnership.
- D) describes a public sector entity.

mcqs.question: Gross profit is best defined as:
options: A) Sales less all expenses of the business
B) Net sales less cost of sales
C) Total income less drawings
D) Sales less returns outwards only
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because gross profit is the difference between the sale proceeds of the period and the cost of the goods actually sold, with no deduction of indirect expenses.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) describes net profit, not gross profit.
- C) drawings are not an expense and never feature in profit computation.
- D) ignores purchases, stock movements, carriage inwards and returns inwards.

mcqs.question: Using the Mr. Karanja data (sales Sh.7,748,400; returns inwards Sh.178,000; purchases Sh.6,666,600; carriage inwards Sh.134,000; returns outwards Sh.99,000; closing stock Sh.1,497,800; first year in business), what is the gross profit?
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: A) Sh.2,366,600 because net sales = 7,748,400 - 178,000 = 7,570,400; cost of sales = 6,666,600 + 134,000 - 99,000 - 1,497,800 = 5,203,800; gross profit = 7,570,400 - 5,203,800 = 2,366,600.

Why the others are wrong:
- B) forgets to deduct returns inwards from sales.
- C) wrongly deducts carriage inwards as if it were carriage outwards.
- D) adds returns outwards to cost of sales instead of deducting them.

mcqs.question: Carriage inwards and carriage outwards are treated respectively as:
options: A) A selling expense and a direct expense
B) A direct expense (cost of sales) and a selling/distribution expense
C) Both direct expenses in the trading account
D) Both selling expenses in the profit and loss account
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because carriage inwards brings goods to the point of sale (part of cost of sales) while carriage outwards distributes goods to customers (a selling expense).

Why the others are wrong:
- A) reverses the two treatments.
- C) and D) put both in the same section, which misstates gross profit.

mcqs.question: Closing stock is valued at:
options: A) Selling price
B) The higher of cost and market price
C) Cost or market price, whichever is lower
D) Historical cost always
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: C) because the study text states that stock is valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower (the prudence concept: never carry stock above its recoverable amount).

Why the others are wrong:
- A) valuing at selling price would anticipate profit.
- B) reverses the prudence rule.
- D) ignores the market-price ceiling.

mcqs.question: Closing stock given as additional information (not in the trial balance) is:
options: A) Shown only in the statement of financial position
B) Credited to the trading account and shown as a current asset
C) Debited to the trading account only
D) Ignored until the following year
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because closing stock outside the trial balance must be brought in with Dr. Closing stock / Cr. Income statement, and it is a current asset.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) applies only when closing stock already appears in the trial balance.
- C) reverses the entry.
- D) would understate both profit and assets.

mcqs.question: An abnormal loss of stock by fire is treated by:
options: A) Leaving it in cost of sales as a normal cost
B) Crediting the trading account in full and charging the loss to the profit and loss account
C) Deducting it from sales
D) Writing it off directly against capital
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because the trading account is prepared under normal conditions and has no place for abnormal events; the loss is charged below gross profit.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) distorts gross profit with an abnormal item.
- C) confuses a stock loss with a sales return.
- D) bypasses the income statement entirely.

mcqs.question: Goods sold on approval, still with the customer unapproved at year-end, are treated by:
options: A) Leaving the sale and debtor in the books
B) Cancelling the sale at selling price and adding the goods to closing stock at cost
C) Writing the goods off as a bad debt
D) Treating the goods as drawings
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because no sale has occurred until approval: Dr. Sales / Cr. Debtors at selling price, and Dr. Stock / Cr. Income statement at cost.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) overstates both sales and debtors.
- C) the customer owes nothing yet, so there is no bad debt.
- D) the owner did not take the goods.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the trial balance and the statement of financial position is TRUE?
options: A) Both are prepared before the income statement
B) The trial balance contains closing stock but the statement of financial position does not
C) The trial balance is prepared before the income statement; the statement of financial position is prepared after it
D) Both contain the balances of all accounts including nominal accounts
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: C) because the trial balance is the input to the income statement, while the statement of financial position needs the resulting net profit to update capital.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) reverses the timing of the statement of financial position.
- B) reverses the closing stock treatment.
- D) the statement of financial position contains only asset, liability and capital balances.

mcqs.question: KASNEB expects assets and liabilities to be marshalled in the:
options: A) Order of liquidity
B) Order of permanence
C) Alphabetical order
D) Order of materiality
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because the study text states the order of permanence (non-current assets first; capital, then long-term, then current liabilities) is the commonly used method.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) liquidity order is the alternative method, not the expected one.
- C) and D) are not recognised marshalling methods.

mcqs.question: Quick (liquid) assets are computed as:
options: A) Current assets plus stock
B) Current assets less stock and prepayments
C) Total assets less current liabilities
D) Cash plus non-current assets
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because quick assets are current assets convertible into cash almost immediately without loss, which excludes stock and prepayments.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) adds the least liquid current asset instead of removing it.
- C) describes net current assets (working capital).
- D) mixes non-current assets into a short-term measure.

mcqs.question: A contingent liability that is probable and reasonably estimable is:
options: A) Disclosed by footnote only
B) Recorded with a journal entry
C) Ignored completely
D) Deducted from the related asset
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because accounting rules require a journal entry when the contingency is both probable and estimable.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) applies when the liability is only possible (not probable) or not estimable.
- C) applies when the contingency is remote.
- D) is not an accounting treatment for contingencies.

mcqs.question: In the statement of financial position, the owner's interest is shown as:
options: A) Capital less net profit plus drawings
B) Capital plus net profit less drawings
C) Capital plus drawings less net loss
D) Net profit less drawings only
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because profit increases the owner's stake while drawings (cash or kind) reduce it.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) reverses the effects of profit and drawings.
- C) adds drawings instead of deducting them.
- D) omits the opening capital balance.

mcqs.question: Salaries of Sh.1,350,000 were paid during the year and Sh.90,000 was accrued at year-end. The correct treatment is:
options: A) Charge Sh.1,350,000 to the income statement only
B) Charge Sh.1,440,000 to the income statement and show Sh.90,000 as a current liability
C) Charge Sh.1,260,000 to the income statement and show Sh.90,000 as a current asset
D) Charge Sh.1,440,000 to the income statement with no statement-of-financial-position entry
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because the accrued expense was incurred in the year (matching concept): Dr. Salaries / Cr. Accrued salaries.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) understates the expense by ignoring the accrual.
- C) deducts the accrual and misclassifies it as an asset.
- D) omits the liability leg of the double entry.

mcqs.question: Rent paid of Sh.480,000 includes Sh.60,000 relating to next year. The correct treatment is:
options: A) Charge Sh.480,000 to the income statement
B) Charge Sh.420,000 to the income statement and show Sh.60,000 as a current asset
C) Charge Sh.540,000 to the income statement
D) Charge Sh.420,000 to the income statement and show Sh.60,000 as a current liability
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) because the prepaid portion has not been incurred: Dr. Prepaid rent / Cr. Rent, leaving Sh.420,000 as the year's charge and Sh.60,000 as a current asset.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) overstates the expense by the prepayment.
- C) adds the prepayment instead of deducting it.
- D) misclassifies the prepayment as a liability.

mcqs.question: Equipment costing Sh.800,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum on the reducing-balance basis. Depreciation for year 2 is:
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: B) Sh.128,000 because year 1 depreciation = 20% x 800,000 = 160,000, leaving NBV of 640,000; year 2 = 20% x 640,000 = 128,000.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) is the year 1 charge.
- C) applies 20% to cost (straight-line thinking).
- D) is 20% of 480,000, which is not the year 2 opening NBV.

mcqs.question: Debtors are Sh.950,000, provision for bad debts in the trial balance is Sh.40,000, and the required provision is 5% of debtors. The income statement charge is:
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: C) Sh.7,500 because the new provision = 5% x 950,000 = 47,500, which exceeds the old provision of 40,000 by 7,500; only the increase is charged.

Why the others are wrong:
- A) charges the full new provision, ignoring the existing one.
- B) leaves the provision unchanged.
- D) adds old and new provisions together.

mcqs.question: Goods costing Sh.40,000 taken by the owner for personal use (not recorded) are adjusted by:
options: A) Dr. Drawings 40,000 / Cr. Purchases 40,000
B) Dr. Purchases 40,000 / Cr. Drawings 40,000
C) Dr. Drawings 40,000 / Cr. Sales 40,000
D) No entry - drawings are not recorded
mcqs.explanation:
Correct: A) Dr. Drawings 40,000 / Cr. Purchases 40,000 because drawings in kind reduce purchases at cost and increase the owner's drawings.

Why the others are wrong:
- B) reverses the entry, increasing cost of sales.
- C) records the goods at selling price as if sold, overstating sales.
- D) omitting the entry overstates both purchases and capital.

theory.question: TBS 1 - The trial balance of K. Wanjala as at 31 December 2025 includes: sales Sh.3,200,000; purchases Sh.1,900,000; opening stock Sh.210,000; carriage inwards Sh.60,000; returns inwards Sh.80,000; returns outwards Sh.50,000; salaries Sh.520,000; rent Sh.300,000; insurance Sh.90,000; discount allowed Sh.25,000; discount received Sh.40,000; debtors Sh.600,000; motor vehicle at cost Sh.900,000. Additional information: (1) Closing stock Sh.260,000. (2) Rent prepaid Sh.30,000. (3) Salaries accrued Sh.45,000. (4) Depreciate the motor vehicle at 10% per annum on cost. Required: prepare the income statement for the year ended 31 December 2025, showing gross profit and net profit.
theory.model:
**Model answer**

```
K. Wanjala - Income Statement for the year ended 31 December 2025
Sh.
Sales 3,200,000 - returns inwards 80,000 = net sales 3,120,000
Cost of sales: opening stock 210,000 + purchases 1,900,000 + carriage inwards 60,000 = 2,170,000;
  less returns outwards 50,000 = 2,120,000; less closing stock 260,000 = 1,860,000
Gross profit = 3,120,000 - 1,860,000 = 1,260,000
Add: discount received 40,000 -> 1,300,000
Less: expenses
  Salaries 520,000 + 45,000 accrued = 565,000
  Rent 300,000 - 30,000 prepaid = 270,000
  Insurance 90,000
  Discount allowed 25,000
  Depreciation: motor vehicle 10% x 900,000 = 90,000
  Total expenses = 1,040,000
Net profit = 1,300,000 - 1,040,000 = 260,000
```

All workings shown; gross profit Sh.1,260,000 and net profit Sh.260,000.

theory.question: TBS 2 - Using the D. Achieng worked example in Lesson 3 (net loss Sh.327,500; drawings Sh.340,000 including goods of Sh.40,000; capital Sh.4,500,000): (a) explain why the owner's capital decreased during the year despite no additional drawings of cash beyond Sh.300,000; (b) state the total current assets and total current liabilities in the statement of financial position, and verify the accounting equation.
theory.model:
**Model answer**

(a) Capital fell because the business made a net loss of Sh.327,500 (which reduces the owner's stake) and total drawings were Sh.340,000 - Sh.300,000 cash plus Sh.40,000 of goods taken in kind. Drawings in kind are real drawings: they reduce purchases (and hence raise gross profit) but are debited to drawings, reducing capital. So capital = 4,500,000 - 327,500 - 340,000 = Sh.3,832,500.

(b) Current assets = stock 510,000 + debtors 902,500 + bank 640,000 + cash 85,000 + prepayments 75,000 = Sh.2,212,500. Current liabilities = creditors 720,000 + accrued salaries 90,000 + accrued interest 50,000 = Sh.860,000. Accounting equation: total assets = 3,480,000 + 2,212,500 = 5,692,500; capital + liabilities = 3,832,500 + 1,000,000 + 860,000 = 5,692,500. Balanced.
